offence_severity: Life imprisonment and fine of Rs. 50,000/- each
physical_harm: Deceased died as a result of being belaboured by the accused
number_of_offences: Charged with multiple offences, but only the charge under Section 302 r/w. s.34 IPC was upheld
key_evidence_accepted: The Supreme Court accepted that the prosecution's case was full of inconsistencies and infirmities, and that the FIR was a post-investigation document. It also noted that the disclosure statements and recovery of weapons were not properly proved under Section 27 of the Evidence Act.
witness_credibility: The court assessed the main witnesses as unreliable, noting contradictions in their testimonies, inherent loopholes, and that the complainant's testimony suffered from patent infirmities and contradictions. The court also found that the witnesses had motives to falsely implicate the accused.

legal_representation.accused: Basavaprabhu S. Patil, Sr. Adv., Geet Ahuja, Anirudh Sanganeria, Samarth Kashyap, Aman Banka, Advs.
legal_representation.state: Aman Panwar, A.A.G., V. N. Raghupathy, Manendra Pal Gupta, Shivam Singh Baghal, Harsh Gattani, Advs.

appeal_history.high_court: Reversed acquittal of A-1, A-2 and A-3 and convicted them
appeal_history.supreme_court: Reversed High Court's judgment and acquitted accused

prosecution_argument: The prosecution argued that the accused A-1, A-2, A-3 and A-4 armed with weapons attacked the victim-son of PW-1, leading to his death. PW-1 ran away, hid behind bushes, returned to his village, and filed a written complaint. The charge-sheet was filed, and the High Court reversed the acquittal of A-1, A-2 and A-3 and convicted them under Section 302 r/w. s.34 IPC.
defence_argument: The defence argued that the prosecution's case was full of inconsistencies, contradictions, and infirmities. The trial court correctly acquitted the accused as the prosecution failed to prove the charges beyond all manner of doubt. The High Court's reversal was not justified as it acted as a first court on independent appreciation of evidence.
legal_principle_applied: The Supreme Court applied the legal principle that the scope of interference by an appellate Court for reversing the judgment of acquittal must be exercised within the four corners of the principles of patent perversity, misreading/omission to consider material evidence, and only one reasonable view being possible.
precedent_relied_upon: Rajesh Prasad v. State of Bihar and Another [2022] 3 SCR 1046 : (2022) 3 SCC 471; H.D. Sundara & Ors. v. State of Karnataka [2023] 14 SCR 47 : (2023) 9 SCC 581; Mohd. Abdul Hafeez v. State of Andhra Pradesh (1983) 1 SCC 143; Subramanya v. State of Karnataka [2022] 14 SCR 828 : 2022 SCC Online SC 1400; State of Uttar Pradesh v. Deoman Upadhyaya [1961] 1 SCR 14 : AIR (1960) SC 1125; Ramanand @ Nandlal Bharti v. State of Uttar Pradesh [2022] 5 SCR 162 : (2022) SCC OnLine SC 1396
